Why Were Webhooks Introduced?


Before diving into the concept of webhooks, let’s explore some foundational terms to understand why webhooks are important, how they differ from APIs, and the problems they solve.
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a way for a client (like a frontend app) and server (like a backend service) to communicate using the HTTP protocol. The client sends an HTTP request to the server, and the server responds—usually with data in JSON or XML format.
📘 Want to know more about APIs? Check this out: API Docs

Boot into Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE).
Swap utilman.exe with cmd.exe on *C:*.
On the login screen, hit Ease of Access → instant SYSTEM cmd.
Run: net user "YourUser" NewPass123!.
Log in, then restore utilman.exe to close the backdoor.
Done. No USB sticks, no reinstall.
:: WinRE Command Prompt (assumes Windows on C:)
bcdedit | find "osdevice"                :: optional sanity check
copy C:\Windows\System32\utilman.exe C:\Windows\System32\utilman.bak
copy C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe     C:\Windows\System32\utilman.exe
exit                                      :: reboot

:: Login screen → Ease of Access shell

articles.author: Feel theFiya
articles.description:
Plan


Over the course of the next few weeks I plan on building a basic operating system in rust. I have no experience in rust, so this is a fairly large hill, and potentially an even bigger boulder. I also have little to no experience in low level programming, save the sprinkle of C++ that I've picked up. However, I did really enjoy the small amount that I've done so I'm excited to see where this takes me. I recently read a book about super learning and that might be the culprit for my current optimism. 
I'm going to post on here weekly with a progress report sort of thing which will outline progress (if any) that I make over the 7 days, as well as other bits such as challenges faced or questions I may have. I will be delighted if one singular person gives feedback at any point during the process, even if it's just to tell me how badly I'm doing :)   
Why am I doing this to myself? It's a mix of 2 things. Firstly, I would one day like to be a semi-competent software developer and this is an area that interests me. I find that writing something down helps me understand it better, as I need to describe it succinctly, and in such a way that someone who cannot read my thoughts can understand it. Secondly, I want to use this as an outlet to improve my  writing and hopefully as a byproduct of that, my own thinking. I believe that developing clear and concise writing will lead to a similar style of thinking, something which I would like to wield. 
If you made it this far, thank you, and if this has (for some reason) intrigued you, check back here every Friday at 12:00 GMT. This is the deadline I've set for myself every week or else I wont do it :)
Beir Bua
articles.title: Writing an OS in Rust

articles.description:
Calling a non-async-signal-safe function from a signal handler is essentially an undefined behaviour and can lead to all sorts of weird behaviours: deadlocks, race conditions and even memory corruption. You may even experience crashes originating from libc, such as the following:
malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted

Fatal glibc error: malloc.c:2599 (sysmalloc): assertion failed: (old_top == initial_top (av) && old_size == 0) || ((unsigned long) (old_size) >= MINSIZE && prev_inuse (old_top) && ((unsigned long) old_end & (pagesize - 1)) == 0)

Signals are a way to do asynchronous messages on a POSIX system (such as BSD, Linux, macOS) to notify a process that a specific event happened. The key feature here is the asynchronous part. A signal can be delivered at almost any moment in…
articles.title: Signal safety and why should you care

I’ve been maintaining a library for my own SaaS that handles role-based access control (RBAC) on both the client and server side. It worked well, but I wanted to push its performance even further. Specifically, I was aiming for:
Faster permission checks – Moving from linear scans to bit-level operations
More efficient memory usage – From O(n) arrays to O(1) bitmaps
Better performance overall, especially under heavy load
Working with edge computing completely reshaped how I think about performance. Here are a few things that really stuck:
Memory is limited – You have to cache smartly and keep your footprint small
Data proximity matters – Optimize for fast, local lookups
Predictability is key – Avoid operations that vary in execution time
Permission Checks Now ~10x Faster
